source_defaults.notes: Original candidate responses or direct quotations, read in context. Retained publisher dates precede the primary. Reporter summaries, allegations and claimed policy effects are not independently verified or substituted for the candidate's own words.

sources.speaker: Robert L. Langford
sources.identity_notes: The source identifies Rob Langford as the Democratic Clark County district-attorney candidate facing Steve Wolfson in2018, matching the canonical Robert L. Langford record.

sources.speaker: Irma Marianela Corado
sources.identity_notes: The publisher names Irma Corado and James Walkinshaw as the two2019 Democratic Braddock District candidates; the canonical record includes Corado's middle name.

sources.speaker: James Robert Walkinshaw
sources.identity_notes: The same questionnaire identifies James Walkinshaw in the2019 Braddock District primary, matching the canonical name with an additional middle name.

sources.speaker: Myles G. Baker
sources.identity_notes: The original candidate-response article identifies Myles Baker as the Democrat running for Larimer County Commissioner District3 in2020. The canonical record includes his middle initial.

statements.quote: If you were not a flight risk and you are not a danger to the community, you shouldn't be in jail
statements.claim: Supports releasing defendants who present neither flight risk nor danger rather than jailing them because of inability to pay.

statements.quote: If you're not a flight risk or danger, you're released.
statements.claim: Supports release under a risk-assessment approach when defendants are not a flight or danger risk.

statements.quote: it's the working poor
statements.claim: Criticizes the cash-bail system for imposing costs and detention on poor defendants. His full answer explains the nonrefundable fee burden rather than merely invoking an ideological label.

statements.quote: I don't know if ending an entire cash bail system is the way to go.
statements.claim: Is unsure about abolishing the entire system and favors risk assessment; separately acknowledges too many people are jailed because they cannot afford premiums.

statements.quote: You have more resources to spend on other cases.
statements.claim: Argues that reducing death-penalty litigation would free resources for other prosecutions. This does not establish a categorical abolition pledge.

statements.quote: giving the jury the option
statements.claim: Defends seeking capital punishment in eligible cases so juries can decide, while disputing the resource argument against it. Legal and cost claims remain attributed.

statements.quote: we're okay with finding that out so we can change it
statements.claim: Emphasizes openness to finding institutional bias and racial disparities as a condition of reform. His expectations are not independently established findings about the office.

statements.quote: We're more reactionary than visionary.
statements.claim: Acknowledges slow reform and a reactive system, rather than asserting the office needs no change.

statements.quote: restoring the Penny for Affordable Housing fund
statements.claim: Supports restoring the named fund and partnerships to create and preserve affordable housing.

statements.quote: restoring and expanding the Penny for Affordable Housing fund
statements.claim: Supports expanding dedicated funding, with separate allocations for new construction and preservation, and more housing near Metro.

statements.quote: I believe housing diversity is a key step
statements.claim: Supports housing diversity in neighborhoods with fewer lower-income residents, connecting it to opportunity and reducing segregation.

statements.quote: Yes.
statements.claim: Answers yes to the immediately preceding question about increasing housing diversity in more affluent parts of the county, and explains support for mixed-income developments.

statements.quote: identify more commuter parking lots
statements.claim: Emphasizes commuter parking, organized carpools and broader transit coverage, including workers outside usual peak hours.

statements.quote: Invest in VRE capital improvements
statements.claim: Prioritizes VRE capacity, Braddock Road improvements without widening, and an I-66 transit option. Studying bus rapid transit is not presented as a committed completed project.

statements.quote: prioritize affordable housing
statements.claim: Supports mixed-use, transit-accessible development with affordability and safeguards against displacement of existing communities.

statements.quote: build neighborhood support on a project-by-project basis
statements.claim: Supports addressing housing shortages while considering project merits and building neighborhood support.

statements.quote: approaches that are least punitive
statements.claim: Supports safer street design, multilingual outreach and data-based assessment while emphasizing equity and less punitive enforcement.

statements.quote: incorporate Vision Zero design and engineering standards
statements.claim: Supports incorporating Vision Zero standards into county planning and partnering with the state transportation agency.

statements.quote: continue the progress on I-25 lane expansion and Hwy 34 repair work
statements.claim: Supports the named road projects while saying the county cannot solve congestion solely by paving and must respond to diverse transport needs.

statements.quote: assist with the capital purchases and let cities partner on the cost of operations
statements.claim: Proposes county support for bus capital purchases and intercity operating partnerships to expand regional service.

statements.quote: take 1% ($1.4m) of the property taxes the county keeps and create a grant fund
statements.claim: Proposes using one percent of retained county property-tax revenue to reimburse local fees waived for affordable housing. The dollar figure is his estimate, not an audited forecast.

statements.quote: recovery & resiliency for ALL of Larimer County
statements.claim: Prioritizes pandemic recovery while retaining environmental stewardship, housing, sustainable growth and transportation as longer-term concerns.

statements.quote: the two most imminent issues are Covid-19 and police reform / use of force
statements.claim: Prioritizes pandemic response and police reform while preserving housing, transit and water as core concerns.

statements.quote: make sure that all voices are heard
statements.claim: Frames governing around volunteer service, constituent voice and collaborative problem-solving across the region.

statements.quote: serving the community and not about bringing ideology into the equation
statements.claim: Frames local government around practical problem-solving, small-town experience and fiscal responsibility.

comparisons.analysis: Both say defendants who present neither flight risk nor danger should be released. This agreement in stated criteria does not establish identical bail procedures.

Langford foregrounds cash bail's burden on poor defendants; Wolfson prefers risk-assessment reform and is unsure about complete abolition. Both acknowledge problems with detention driven by inability to pay.

Langford foregrounds the opportunity cost of capital litigation and redirecting resources; Wolfson foregrounds preserving the jury's option. Langford is not inaccurately coded as pledging blanket abolition.
Langford emphasizes examining institutional bias; Wolfson acknowledges slow, reactive reform. Neither is presented as saying that no systemic changes are needed.
Both support the named affordable-housing fund. Walkinshaw specifies a larger allocation and division between new and preserved housing; Corado's answer does not specify an identical funding amount.
Both explicitly support increasing housing diversity in more affluent parts of the county.
Corado foregrounds everyday commuter access, carpools and off-peak needs; Walkinshaw names rail capacity and specific road/transit corridors. These priorities can complement one another.

Corado foregrounds affordability and anti-displacement safeguards in transit-oriented development; Walkinshaw foregrounds evaluating projects and building local support. Neither answer establishes blanket opposition to building housing.
Both support safer streets and a zero-deaths goal. Corado stresses outreach and least-punitive enforcement alongside design; Walkinshaw stresses engineering standards and state partnership.

Shadduck-McNally names road projects while recognizing broader modal needs; Baker specifies county capital support for regional bus partnerships. These are different proposed tools, not proven opposing positions.

Both foreground pandemic response while retaining long-term concerns. Shadduck-McNally emphasizes recovery and resilience across services; Baker expressly adds police reform as an immediate priority. Omission from a short answer is not opposition.

Shadduck-McNally emphasizes inclusive service and collaboration; Baker emphasizes practical, non-ideological service and fiscal responsibility. Neither answer establishes rejection of the other's stated values.
